title: Events & delegation
canDo: respond to clicks, including on dynamically-added elements

blocks.md: Your page is static until it *listens*. Events are how the browser tells your code that something happened — a click, a keypress, a form submission. Once you can attach a listener and read what was clicked, your pages stop being brochures and start being apps.

blocks.canDo: respond to clicks, including on dynamically-added elements

blocks.md:
**Three things to nail this session:**

1. **`addEventListener`** — the right way to attach a handler: `element.addEventListener('click', fn)`. Avoid inline `onclick` attributes.
2. **The event object** — every handler receives an `event` (or `e`) argument automatically. `event.target` is the *exact* element that was clicked; `event.preventDefault()` stops default behaviour (e.g. form submissions, link navigation).
3. **Event delegation** — instead of attaching one listener per element, attach *one listener to a parent* and check `event.target` inside it. Because events bubble up the DOM tree, the parent sees every click on its children — including elements added to the DOM *after* the listener was set up. This is how you handle dynamic lists without re-binding listeners every time you add a row.

blocks.md: The most common mistake is attaching listeners inside a loop — one per item — and then wondering why adding new items breaks things. The delegation pattern (one listener on the parent) sidesteps the whole problem. If you find yourself writing `forEach(item => item.addEventListener(...))`, pause and ask whether a parent listener would be cleaner.

questions.question: What is the preferred way to attach a click handler to a button in modern JavaScript?
options: Set the button's `onclick` attribute in HTML: `<button onclick="handler()">`
questions.explanation: `addEventListener` is the standard, flexible approach — it lets you attach multiple listeners to the same element and remove them cleanly, unlike the `onclick` property or HTML attribute.

questions.question: Inside an event handler, what does `event.target` refer to?
options: The element that the `addEventListener` call was made on
The element that the user actually interacted with (the origin of the event)
The parent element of the clicked element
The `document` object, which receives all events
questions.explanation: `event.target` is the innermost element the user clicked. `event.currentTarget` is the element the listener is attached to — these differ when delegation is used.

questions.question: You have a `<ul>` that gets new `<li>` items added dynamically. Which approach correctly handles clicks on both existing and future list items?
options: Loop over all current `<li>` elements and call `addEventListener('click', ...)` on each one
Attach one `addEventListener('click', ...)` to the `<ul>` and check `event.target` inside the handler
Use `setInterval` to re-attach listeners every second so new items are covered
Attach the listener to `document.body` and rely on `event.currentTarget` to identify the item
questions.explanation: Event delegation — a single listener on the parent `<ul>` — works for current and future children because click events bubble up through the DOM. Looping over existing items misses anything added later.

blocks.md: You can now attach event listeners properly, read the event object, and use delegation to handle dynamically-added elements with a single parent listener. Next up: the array methods that power dynamic lists.
